title: Chemical Safety
summary: Every hazardous chemical must come with a Safety Data Sheet in a standard 16-section format. Workers can use it to learn the hazards, protective measures, and emergency steps for the chemicals they handle.
talking_points: The Hazard Communication Standard requires manufacturers, distributors, or importers to provide a Safety Data Sheet (SDS) for each hazardous chemical.
Every SDS uses the same 16-section format, so you can find information quickly.
Sections 1 to 8 give the quick-use information: identification, hazards, ingredients, first aid, fire-fighting, spill response, handling and storage, and exposure controls and PPE.
Section 2 lists the hazard class, signal word, hazard statements, pictograms, and precautionary statements.
Section 4 gives first-aid steps by route of exposure: inhalation, skin and eye contact, and ingestion.
Section 6 covers spills and leaks, including protective equipment and cleanup. Section 7 covers safe handling and storage, including incompatible chemicals.
Section 8 lists exposure limits, engineering controls such as local exhaust ventilation, and the PPE to wear, such as the right glove material.
Read the SDS before you use a new chemical (good practice). Section 7 may include hygiene rules for the chemical, such as no eating, drinking, or smoking in work areas.
site_hazards_to_check: Chemicals on site with no SDS available
SDSs kept where workers cannot get to them quickly
Containers with missing or unreadable labels
Work areas without the ventilation or PPE the SDS calls for
Eating, drinking, or smoking in chemical work areas where the SDS or site rules prohibit it
discussion_questions: Where do we keep the SDSs for the chemicals on this job?
Which SDS section tells you what PPE to wear, and which tells you what to do in a spill?
What is the first-aid step if this chemical gets in your eyes?

attribution.notice: Adapted from OSHA published material. Reproduced with attribution for jobsite safety training; not an endorsement by OSHA.

flags: Verified against OSHA 3514 (Hazard Communication: Safety Data Sheets brief): 16-section format, description of Sections 1-8, Section 2 label elements, Section 4 route-of-exposure first aid, Section 6/7/8 contents (incompatibles, local exhaust ventilation, glove material) all in source.

FIX: original last point stated 'Eating, drinking, and smoking in work areas is prohibited where chemicals are handled' as a general rule and 'Read the SDS before you use a new chemical' as if sourced. The source only gives eating/drinking/smoking as an example of hygiene guidance an SDS may contain in Section 7. Reworded accordingly and labelled the read-before-use point as good practice; matching hazard item softened.

Citations: 29 CFR 1926.59 exists and is the construction Hazard Communication section (it adopts 1910.1200 for construction); 1910.1200 is the text the source cites and applies to construction through 1926.59. Both accurate. Not in the source: 1926.59 (structurer-added, verified correct).
Non-blocking: point 1 says the standard puts the duty on manufacturers/distributors/importers to provide the SDS; employer duty to keep SDSs accessible is in TBT-110.
